description_full: Daktronics, Inc. designs, manufactures, and sells electronic display systems and related solutions for sports, commercial, and transportation applications in the United States and internationally. It operates through Commercial, Live Events, High School Park and Recreation, Transportation, and International segments. The company offers video display and walls; sport scoreboard solutions; LED message displays and sings; intelligent transportation systems dynamic message signs; mass transit display; sound systems; and digital billboards and street furniture, and digit and price displays. It also provides indoor dynamic messaging systems; and software and controllers, which includes Venus, a control suite software to efficiently distribute and update content across single or multiple displays. The company serves out-of-home companies, retailers, quick-serve restaurants, casinos, shopping centers, cruise ships, commercial building owners, petroleum retailers, governmental transportation departments, transportation industry contractors, airlines, and sports and commercial business facilities. It sells its products through direct sales and resellers. Daktronics, Inc. was incorporated in 1968 and is headquartered in Brookings, South Dakota.

financial_summary: Daktronics, Inc. is a small-cap technology business with a $926M market cap on $839M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 10% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 24% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $34M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.08× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 42× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.9% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.3× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 7% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 32% below the high.

val: The stock trades 40% below its DCF fair value of $31.88, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 14%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.47 to $53.62 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 19.7 vs 27.4 and EV/EBITDA 9.9 vs 17.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 43% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.6% (vs the 8% bar).

prof: ROIC of 18% clears the cost of capital of 10.0% by 8pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.96).
It runs a 24% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 8/9 and cash conversion of 1.08x.
ROE of 15% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 5.2% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $120.9M (13% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.1, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years, 11.7% over 5 years and 3.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 85% of profits supports about 15.3% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -10.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.02 and a backlog worth 51% of annual revenue.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (1.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 15, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 5.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 76%.
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 2 sales over the past year, net $145K sold.
It returns 2.8% a year to shareholders (2.8% in buybacks).
The share count has grown 1.1% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
people: With about 2,423 employees, each generates about $346K of revenue, in line with the Technology median, and revenue has grown 3.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $554K (2x revenue per employee).
